new_statements.quote: [p. 52, sec. 2.2.1 'Main-stress'; PDF p. 55:] Germanic main-stress invariably goes on the initial syllable of the stem. The locus of main-stress is thus determined on morphological grounds, which means that there is no need to refer to previous prosodic structure in assigning main-stress; all we need is a stem morpheme, a content word. [p. 99, sec. 3.1.2 'Foot-algorithm'; PDF p. 102:] The iamb, too, is clearly incorrect for Germanic. Germanic main-stress invariably goes on the initial stem-syllable, which in the vast majority of cases is the word-initial syllable. This is not an expected feature of an iambic system. Also, main-stress is clearly trochaic, since otherwise words like *dagaz 'day' would have final stress. [p. 246, sec. 5.2.1; PDF p. 249:] (8) The stress system in late Proto-Nordic a. new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Antonsen 2002: Germanic accent shift to the root syllable in all cases = fixed initial/root stress, initial stress); Riad adds the explicit stem-initial (morphological, weight-insensitive) formulation for Proto-Nordic, the secondary-stress algorithm (moraic trochees left-to-right, weight-sensitive, clash destressing) and the unstressed-prefix proviso. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Germanic as reflected in Gothic and Proto-Nordic (the language of the older runic inscriptions), main stress falls invariably on the initial syllable of the stem, which for the vast majority of words is the word-initial syllable; its location is fixed by morphology (stem morpheme), not by weight ('Main-stress syllable: morphological criterion.. weight insensitive'); main stress is dynamic and trochaic; prefixes are unstressed. The main-stress syllable carries a bimoraic template (word minimality).
new_statements.secondary_stress: After main stress, further (secondary) stresses are assigned by iterating the moraic (quantitative) trochee left to right, weight-sensitively (in non-initial syllables only sonorants are moraic); the rightmost stress is removed under stress clash (destressing), which Riad uses to derive vowel shortening; long vowels in non-initial syllables receive prominent positions; e.g. late PN ketill, hamarr get a final-syllable stress that blocks final syncope but is destressed when adjacent to main stress (pp. 98-106, 246-247).
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixes are unstressed (stem-initial, not word-initial, stress; Gothic ga-, Late OSw be-, for- loans cited); no lexical exceptions to initial main stress are given; light-stem bisyllables (*katilaz type) split the main-stress foot over two syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Riad's object is the reconstructed Germanic prosodic system 'as reflected in Gothic and Proto-Nordic' and its Nordic continuation (Proto-Nordic = the language of the older runic inscriptions, c. 200-800, through Old Swedish); the stress statements quoted are made for Germanic/Proto-Nordic generally and restated as 'the stress system in late Proto-Nordic' (sec. 5.2.1); runic evidence is used for the syncope chronology (sec. 3.2.1).

tone.quote: The traditional and best known hypothesis (Oftedal's 'Hypothesis A') is that the pitch accent distinction is of Old Scandinavian origin (1000–1200 AD, but possibly even later). ... The second hypothesis (Oftedal's 'Hypothesis B') is due ultimately to Kock (1901). Kock pointed out data which could not be explained according to the Old Scandinavian Hypothesis and attempted to trace the distinction back to the Syncope Period of Proto-Nordic (800–850 AD). ... This article essentially a response to Riad and argues the case of the Old Scandinavian Hypothesis.

sources.note: As summarized in Bye 2004 sec. 4.1 and Riad 2023 sec. 2: argues the accent 1/2 distinction arose in Old Scandinavian (c. 1000-1200) when cliticization of the definite article and epenthesis created new disyllables with accent 1, and shows Kock's Proto-Nordic syncope account fails for comparatives and minnr-type forms; i.e. no tonal distinction is attributed to Proto-Norse. Not opened.
